articles.desc: Nasdaq 100 suffers worst day since 2020 Magnificent 7: What are the technicals telling traders for each of those companies him WTI crude oil settles at $90.52, up 2.72% as buyers defend key support Non-farm payrolls preview: October numbers show a skew Europe Close: AI and chip liquidation drags equ
articles.content: Nasdaq 100 suffers worst day since 2020 Magnificent 7: What are the technicals telling traders for each of those companies him WTI crude oil settles at $90.52, up 2.72% as buyers defend key support Non-farm payrolls preview: October numbers show a skew Europe Close: AI and chip liquidation drags equities lower in US, but Europe is mixed. Bitcoin falls with risk off sentiment. The price is testing a key swing area target. The market is telling the hyperscalers it's happy about a slower data center buildout Crude oil tests the key confluence area and finds willing buyers Fed's Barkin: Gradual pace of hikes "makes sense" Marco Rubio ‘on resignation watch’ - report Fed's Hammack: Gradual rate hikes are the best way to get inflation to target US Q3 productivity +3.6% vs +2.8% expected US initial jobless claims 189K vs 196K estimate Morning Kickstart: BOE hikes to 4% as sterling struggles to hold its gains investingLive European news wrap: BoE raises bank rate to 4.00% as expected BoE Governor Bailey says there is a case for another 25bps hike if war doesn't end Wednesday’s rotation out of AI and into the broader market turned into a broad selloff on Thursday. The Nasdaq 100 took the biggest hit, but the Russell 2000 fell 4.45% and the Dow lost more than it gained the day before. Falling Treasury yields helped gold catch a bid. They did little for tech stocks or Bitcoin. Crude went the other way. After Wednesday’s plunge on hopes for an end to the Iran war, reports of fresh Gulf shipping incidents put the risk to supplies back in focus. The dollar was mixed, with the Australian dollar taking the biggest hit among the majors and the yen holding up best. The dollar gains against the Aussie but loses ground to the yen The USD was strongest against the AUD, with AUDUSD down 1.13% to 0.6925. It was weakest against the JPY, with USDJPY down 0.49% to 157.64. Lower U.S. yields were consistent with the move in USDJPY, while the Aussie fell alongside other risk-sensitive assets. Elsewhere, EURUSD fell 0.09% to 1.1217, GBPUSD fell 0.17% to 1.3448, and NZDUSD fell 0.50% to 0.5592. USDCAD rose 0.31% to 1.4020 despite the rebound in crude, while USDCHF edged down 0.02% to 0.8166. Treasury yields fall, led by the 2-year 2-year yield 4.4665%, down 11.45 basis points 5-year yield 4.6098%, down 7.82 basis points 10-year yield 4.8408%, down 5.12 basis points 30-year yield 5.2581%, down 2.19 basis points The curve steepened as short-term yields fell more than long-term yields. The size of the move at the front end stood out given that jobless claims came in below expectations and crude bounced. U.S. stocks close sharply lower Dow industrial average −1,833.16 points (−3.44%) to 51,528.16 S&P 500 −334.77 points (−4.35%) to 7,353.85 Nasdaq Composite −1,421.52 points (−5.52%) to 24,315.00 Russell 2000 −127.11 points (−4.45%) to 2,729.84 Nasdaq 100 −1,807.36 points (−6.36%) to 26,629.81 AI suppliers lead the selloff The selling hit memory, storage, chip equipment and data-center suppliers. Micron was down about 12% during the session as investors questioned how quickly the AI buildout would translate into orders for suppliers. That matters across the supply chain, from the memory that goes into AI accelerators to the drives that store the data. All seven Magnificent 7 stocks were lower in my late-session check. Nvidia and Tesla were the only two underperforming both Nasdaq indices at that point. Apple and Alphabet held up best, down 1.27% and 1.53%, respectively. Magnificent 7 coverage Europe closes mixed Spain’s IBEX 35 +0.59% France’s CAC 40 +0.34% Germany’s DAX −0.43% U.K.’s FTSE 100 −0.43% Italy’s FTSE MIB −1.03% InvestingLive’s European close U.S. data hold up as markets look to Washington Initial jobless claims fell to 189,000 versus 196,000 expected, while third-quarter productivity rose 3.6% versus 2.8% expected. In the U.K., the Bank of England raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to 4.00%, citing inflation pressure tied to the Middle East conflict and higher energy prices. Sterling still slipped against the dollar. After the European close, Adam Button highlighted two questions coming out of the midterms. Will the Trump administration change course on Iran, and will it move to ease tariffs as Congress presses for changes? The answers matter for oil supply risk and for the inflation outlook. InvestingLive’s Washington coverage Crude rebounds as Gulf shipping risks resurface WTI futures settled at $90.52 a barrel, up $2.40 or 2.72%, and were quoted later at $91.06, up 3.34%. Wednesday’s drop of more than 8% reflected hopes for a path out of the Iran war. On Thursday, reports of several shipping incidents in the Gulf reminded traders that the risk to supply is still there. Treasury yields fell even as crude recovered. WTI settlement and Gulf shipping coverage Gold gains while silver and copper fall Spot gold rose 0.68% to $4,088.02. Lower Treasury yields reduced the opportunity cost of holding gold, and the equity selloff was consistent with some demand for a haven. Silver fell 0.94% to $51.76 and copper dropped 3.51% to $6.2035. The weakness in those two was consistent with their greater exposure to industrial demand. Bitcoin gives back its rebound Bitcoin was down 5.69% at $75,861 late in the session. It rallied alongside stocks on Wednesday and fell alongside them on Thursday, trading much more like the Nasdaq than gold. See technical post here. What carries into Friday The first question is whether buyers return to the chip and data-center names that led the market lower. I’ll also be watching whether the 2-year yield holds onto its decline and whether crude keeps its rebound. If Gulf shipping risks keep oil bid while short-term yields stay under pressure, that will be a divergence worth following. This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Planning approval paves way for vital wastewater upgrade in Limerick town
articles.desc: Construction in Askeaton is expected to begin in the second half of 2027
articles.content: Planning approval paves way for vital wastewater upgrade in Limerick town Planning approval paves way for vital wastewater upgrade in Limerick town Construction in Askeaton is expected to begin in the second half of 2027 ’s wastewater infrastructure have taken an important step forward, with receiving planning permission for the project in the west This upgrade will increase wastewater treatment capacity to support new homes and future development in the local community, while providing more sustainable wastewater treatment and helping to protect the local environment. The project will include a new wastewater treatment plant (WwTP) and new wastewater pumping station (WwPS) at Abbey View, together with additional stormwater storage and upgrades to the wastewater network. As part of the works, existing infrastructure at Abbey View and Lismakeera will be replaced or decommissioned. Angus Hall, Uisce Éireann Programme Manager, said: “Receiving planning permission is an important milestone for this essential project and brings us another step closer to delivering the wastewater infrastructure Askeaton needs for the future. “This upgrade will support existing and future development, while delivering more efficient and sustainable wastewater treatment and protecting the local environment. We are progressing procurement and look forward to construction next year.” Construction is expected to begin in the second half of 2027, subject to procurement and governance process. Uisce Éireann is responsible for delivering public drinking water and wastewater services for the people of Ireland. They say they are “committed to enabling communities to thrive by continuously upgrading and developing critical infrastructure to support sustainable growth and development, providing safe drinking water, and enhancing the environment”. articles.title: Investing in a company? The paperwork matters more than you might think
articles.desc: Shareholders’ agreements explained: key rights, voting, dividends, share sales, dispute resolution and due diligence for UK limited company investor
articles.content: Shareholders' agreements protect limited company investors | The Herald Shareholders' agreements protect limited company investors A well-drafted shareholders’ agreement is therefore an important protection for anyone investing in a limited company. This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A well-drafted agreement can protect investments, clarify responsibilities and balance all the interests of everyone involved in a deal Limited companies come in all shapes and sizes. Likewise, their owners can range from an individual with a handful of shares to a partner in the business or a large institutional shareholder, such as a pension scheme. One of the features of a limited company is the flexibility of its ownership. Existing shareholders may wish to increase their stake in the business, while new shareholders can also buy into an established company. There is no general legal requirement for anything in writing beyond the shares themselves. It is possible to buy and sell shares, or issue new shares to shareholders, and simply carry on based on verbal agreements, trust or informal understandings. Let's remember that a company has its own legal identity, separate from its shareholders and directors. Owning a slice of the business does not automatically give or imply control, unless an individual, either alone or together with other shareholders, holds sufficient voting rights to influence the direction the company takes. Common sense and good practice dictate that anyone investing money or other assets in a company should have some protection and the ability to have their voice heard in the management of the business. One standard way of regulating the rights and responsibilities of shareholders is through a shareholders' agreement. This is a legal contract signed by the shareholders, setting out their relationship with the company and with each other. It should cover all stages of share ownership, from the initial purchase, through the ongoing operation of the company, to the eventual sale of shares or winding up of the company, whatever the reason. This could be a successful buyout or, at the other end of the scale, business failure and liquidation. Signing a shareholders' agreement is not the first step in buying into a company. Like other legal documents, such as a property lease, commercial property purchase or mortgage agreement, it is the final stage of a negotiated deal and reflects the rights, responsibilities and financial arrangements agreed between the parties. This means two things. Firstly, negotiations should be thorough and cover all likely eventualities in the life of the company, without leaving gaps or loose ends. Secondly, there are a number of important matters that need to be checked before committing to an investment. These include the financial value of the business, its legal structure, any charges registered against it and its Companies House filings. It's also worth looking at less technical matters, such as the company's ethos, personnel, reputation and standing in the business community. All of these should be properly investigated before any agreement is signed. If you're unsure what to look for or don't fully understand the legal or financial implications, it's sensible to seek professional advice, including legal representation from a solicitor who can help protect your interests. Shareholders' agreements all serve the same basic purpose of governing relationships between shareholders and with the company, but there is no single template. Each agreement can be tailored to the circumstances of the business and its shareholders. articles.title: Odisha Sees Rise In UG Enrolment After Gyanodaya Rollout
articles.desc: Bhubaneswar: Under Graduate (UG) enrolment in Odisha has increased by 14,758 students in the current academic year following the implementation of the
articles.content: Odisha Sees Rise In UG Enrolment After Gyanodaya Rollout | Odisha Odisha Sees Rise In UG Enrolment After Gyanodaya Rollout Under Graduate (UG) enrolment in Odisha has increased by 14,758 students in the current academic year following the implementation of the state government’s Gyanodaya – Free Education from KG to PG scheme, Higher Education Minister Suryabanshi Suraj said on Thursday. The total number of students admitted to regular undergraduate courses rose from 1,64,179 in the previous academic year to 1,78,937 this year, the Minister said while reviewing the functioning of the Higher Education Department at a meeting here. The impact of the scheme has been particularly significant in aspirational districts, which have recorded the highest admission percentages. Kalahandi topped the list with 99.09%, followed by Koraput (98.82%), Balangir (95.57%), Malkangiri (95.37%) and Nuapada (94.64%). The meeting also reviewed the filling up of vacant teaching and non-teaching posts in universities and colleges, recruitment examinations conducted by the State Selection Board (SSB), and the progress of projects under the Pradhan Mantri Uchchatar Shiksha Abhiyan (PM-USHA). To strengthen the administration of government degree colleges, 48 new Principal posts have been created, taking the total number of such posts from 18 to 66 across the state’s 66 government degree colleges. The recruitment process is underway to fill 385 vacant Assistant Professor (Stage-I) posts in various subjects in these colleges. Similarly, universities are undertaking recruitment to fill 1,434 vacant teaching positions, including Assistant Professors, Associate Professors and Professors, across 17 state universities. Following a rationalisation exercise, 262 additional non-teaching and administrative posts have also been created across the 17 universities to improve their functioning. These include 69 Junior Assistants, 37 Senior Assistants, 49 Assistant Librarians, 30 Librarians, 17 Section Officers and other posts in administrative, examination, accounts and library cadres. The State Selection Board has conducted recruitment examinations and declared results for more than 2,800 vacancies across various cadres over the past two years. It has issued notifications this year for recruitment to another 1,557 posts. Expressing satisfaction over the rise in higher education enrolment, particularly in aspirational districts, Suraj said the Gyanodaya scheme was making higher education more accessible and helping strengthen an inclusive education system in the state. The government is committed to improving higher educational institutions and ensuring quality education for all, he said, adding that the newly created posts would be filled soon. The Minister directed departmental officials to ensure effective implementation of various schemes and complete ongoing projects within the stipulated timelines. Higher Education Department Commissioner-cum-Secretary Aravind Agrawal, Director Kali Prasanna Mahapatra and other senior officials attended the meeting. This is an argument over how AI doomerism is impacting our world, our business, our governments and how doomerism is wrong and preventing some of the best of what is to come. On the night of October 17, 2026, a Palestinian flag went up over the Monument à la République in central Paris. The French flag it replaced came down with a crowd cheering below. A car was already burning nearby. By midday the French authorities had counted around 140 protests across the country and more than 32,000 people in the streets. Hundreds were arrested. The town hall in Marseille was breached. The tourist office in Lyon was set on fire. The protests had started weeks earlier over teacher shortages and crumbling school buildings. Roughly 200 schools had been blockaded by students demanding adequate staffing. By the night of the 17th, the schools were not what anyone was talking about. They were talking about Palestine. Something is off with the frame. Start with the most obvious thing. There is no active war in Gaza. The Trump-era twenty-point peace framework was signed. The ceasefire is holding, shakily, into October 2026. If the point of a protest tonight is to stop a war, there are other wars to stop. The one in Ukraine has not stopped. The one in Sudan has displaced more than ten million people and is still accelerating. Neither got a flag on the Monument à la République. France itself is one of the few Western countries that formally called for a Palestinian state. France has among the most generous social programs in the developed world. If you had walked those streets looking for French flags you would have found very few of them, and no demand that the Fifth Republic do anything about French schools at the scale the night was now operating at. The thing that started the march was the thing nobody still in the street was there to talk about. Something else had taken over. If you are leading anything right now, this is for you. For the board member watching her 24-year-old associate quietly lose interest in the career ladder. For the CEO whose engineering Slack has gone sideways about something nobody is paying the company to care about. For the investor whose consumer-sentiment thesis has decoupled from consumer-spending. The street in Paris and the comment thread inside your company are the same story. The mental model you need to read both correctly is what this piece is for. Get it wrong and you will keep misreading your market, your clients, and your people. Get it right and the operating environment every leader is now in starts to make sense. and a nod to Frankenstein. The thing standing in that Paris street is a cause stitched together from borrowed parts, taught to walk on its own, and no longer resembling any of the parts that went into it. Paris is not an isolated case. The same week, students clashed with police in Brussels and Liège. Italian student marches in Turin and Milan turned into looting on Via Torino, with hundreds detained. articles.title: Stormont MLAs to receive lower pay rise than previously suggested
articles.desc: Stormont's Independent Remuneration Board had initially proposed increasing MLAs' annual salary to £69,216.
articles.content: Stormont MLAs to receive more than £1k pay rise - BBC News It has been confirmed that Northern Ireland Assembly members (MLAs) will see their salaries rise by just over £1,300 from next May. Stormont's Independent Remuneration Board had initially proposed increasing MLAs annual salary to £69,216. But on Thursday the board said having taken hundreds of views on board in a public consultation, it would now limit the increase to 2% instead of 3%. Chair of the board, Alan Lowry, said a reduced cap on the annual percentage increase will be put in place after that date, limiting the overall financial impact of the changes. He said the final determination is now being presented to the Assembly Commission for publication and implementation. "We are grateful to more than 270 individuals who took the time to respond to our consultation, providing us with feedback and constructive commentary. "We considered what people told us and, as a result, made significant adjustments to our proposals," he added. "More than nine out of ten respondents told us that the proposed MLA salary was too high and disagreed that it appropriately reflected the complexity and importance of the MLA role." He said the arrangements for the next mandate reflect inflation as well as wider pay trends and therefore involve a more modest financial adjustment. £2k pay rise for MLAs is 'grotesque', says first minister MLAs approve new body to set their salaries No budget resolution reached yet, says O'Neill

articles.title: Talking finances at Thanksgiving doesn't have to be awkward
articles.content: Talking finances at Thanksgiving doesn't have to be awkward – WSB-TV Channel 2 - Atlanta Talking finances at Thanksgiving doesn't have to be awkward If you'll have young adults at your Thanksgiving table, the topic of money could come up this year. Seventy-two percent of U.S. adults under 30 said they feel comfortable talking about finances with family and friends in the of more than 3,200 respondents conducted by . In comparison, only 56% of Millennials feel the same way, along with 47% of Gen Xers and 31% of Boomers. Why the difference? Younger generations may face different financial pressures than older ones, such as starting their careers and families while the cost of living climbs. They also may depend on their parents for financial help, which makes the subject unavoidable. “Social media and increasing transparency have made it easier to talk openly about all kinds of topics, including money, which was considered off-limits,” says Lucia Franco, consumer insights expert at Forbright Bank. She notes that the older adults in the survey tended to be more private about their finances, but younger adults may be able to show older generations the benefits of openly discussing money. As families gather for the holidays, it may be wise to be prepared if the topic comes up. Talking about money can be a relief and even useful. While it may initially feel uncomfortable, it provides a great example and may dispel negative feelings around financial topics. Here’s how to be prepared to talk about money with family and friends if the opportunity arises this holiday season. While it’s not always appropriate to bring up money, it’s possible others need a safe space to share money issues and learn from other family members’ financial experience. Here are a few ways these conversations may be beneficial: Reduce shame and anxiety. Money carries emotional weight, especially when things are tight. Debt, overspending, thin savings, or simply not knowing how any of it works can feel embarrassing. Staying silent rarely fixes it. Saying it out loud and asking for guidance can lift a surprising amount of weight, and you may find you're in good company. Build trust and alignment. Honest conversations with a partner or parent may help surface hidden debt and keep everyone pointed at the same goals. Understanding a parent's finances matters even more if you serve as their executor or power of attorney. Improve financial literacy. Talking through budgets, debt, and income lets you pick up practical tips from people you trust. This is especially good for children and young adults to learn positive financial habits . Parents who talk openly about money may help children build healthy long-term financial habits instead of a fear of scarcity. Enable confidence in pay negotiation. Openness leads to transparency, and transparency is a real tool for . When salary talk moves from awkward to ordinary, it may help people negotiate with more confidence. Ease social pressure. Saying plainly what you can afford makes group dinners, trips, and gifts easier and fairer to plan. These conversations also answer the question most of us have quietly asked at some point: How is everyone else doing this? Learning how friends handle debt, savings, or an advisor relationship teaches everyone something. How to Talk to Family and Friends About Money If you expect to discuss finances with your friends and family members, the goal is to keep it warm and low stakes: less personal, less judgmental, a little humble about your own missteps, and focused on the big picture. Try to set a calm tone and focus on shared values, not dollars. Use "I" statements. Frame things around your own experience, so no one hears blame. Keep numbers private. Leaving exact dollar amounts out makes it easier to talk about goals. Keep advice at a high level. This isn't a financial planning session. articles.title: Is a Roth IRA conversion worth it? The one thing that matters
articles.content: Is a Roth IRA conversion worth it? The one thing that matters – WSB-TV Channel 2 - Atlanta Is a Roth IRA conversion worth it? The one thing that matters Roth and Traditional IRAs can be an important part of retirement planning. In this article, outlines which one may be best suited for you. A Traditional IRA gives you a tax break today. A Roth IRA gives you one in retirement. Converting means paying the tax bill now, so the money comes out completely tax-free later. , that money gets taxed exactly once, at whatever rate applies in the year it happens. So your decision can boil down to one question: Which year has the lower rate, this one or the one you’ll be in when you’d otherwise withdraw it? A Traditional IRA lets you deduct your contribution from that year’s taxable income.The amount you deposit in your IRA account is treated as a reduction to your total income on your tax return. If you have a 401(k) or similar retirement plan at work, your ability to deduct your IRA deposit may be limited depending on your income. You can't withdraw before 59½ without penalty (with ), and RMDs (required minimum distributions) start at 73. Withdrawals are taxed as regular income at whatever rate applies that year. This works out well for people who retire into a lower bracket, though that's not guaranteed. Think of your yearly income as a pie the government takes a slice of as tax. Putting money into a Traditional IRA cuts a piece out of that pie before the government takes its slice — so there’s less pie left to tax. Since less of your income gets taxed, you owe less tax overall. That’s the “break”: you’re not getting free money; you’re just letting less of your income get taxed in the first place. In a way, the Roth IRA is the opposite of the Traditional IRA. You don’t receive a tax deduction for deposits. However, the money can grow tax-free. You can withdraw your direct contributions from a Roth IRA at any time, tax- and penalty-free. Once you have held the account for 5 years and reach age 59 1⁄2, any growth within the account can also be withdrawn tax-free. There are no required distributions at any age. The Roth IRA has its own income limits; for 2026, the phase-out begins at $153,000 for single taxpayers and $242,000 for married filing jointly. With a Roth IRA, it works the other way: The government takes its full slice of your income now, before you set anything aside. But whatever you save after that grows into its own, bigger pie by retirement and the government doesn’t touch that pie. Every bit of the growth is yours. A conversion moves money from a Traditional IRA (or directly from a 401(k)) into a Roth IRA. To do this, you would be required to pay tax on the converted amount. But once that money is part of the Roth IRA, it wouldn’t be subject to tax again. Any conversions from a traditional IRA to a Roth IRA must be done within 60 days to be considered a conversion contribution. The current law also permits a conversion from your 401(k) directly to a Roth account. Assess if you’ll probably be in a higher bracket later. You can’t exactly know your future rate, but you can estimate. Early in your career, your income and tax rate are usually at their lowest.If you’re near retirement, you can add up expected Social Security and pension income for a real number. if you're in the 10%–12% bracket with rising income ahead; you can pay the conversion tax from savings (not the IRA itself), and you have years for the money to grow tax-free. if converting pushes you into a much higher bracket this year, you'd need IRA funds to cover the tax (which can also trigger a penalty), or you expect a lower rate in retirement anyway. Either IRA can be a great way to achieve your retirement planning goals. Your savings decisions are based on your particular financial reality. articles.title: People with Tourette syndrome, like Billie Eilish, use everything in their power to suppress tics. This exhausting process is key to treatment.
articles.content: People with Tourette syndrome, like Billie Eilish, use everything in their power to suppress tics. This exhausting process is key to treatment. – WSB-TV Channel 2 - Atlanta People with Tourette syndrome, like Billie Eilish, use everything in their power to suppress tics. This exhausting process is key to treatment. Imagine trying not to blink, resisting the urge to sneeze or refusing to scratch an intense itch. For a short time, you can probably succeed, but the effort becomes increasingly untenable until the urge eventually wins. People with Tourette syndrome describe tic suppression in a similar manner. Tourette syndrome causes tics, or , that a person cannot always control. These tics often come and go, change over time and may occur along with attention problems, anxiety or obsessive-compulsive behaviors, Dr. Michael Okun, a neurologist at the University of Florida, writes in , based on 20 years of treating people with Tourette's. Some people with Tourette's can temporarily control tics, such as during a public interview, but that does not mean tics are voluntary. Nor does it mean the person is faking their diagnosis. Rather, suppression can be a hallmark of the disorder and, ironically, has become one of the foundations of modern treatment. Yet suppression can come at a cost. Many patients say they can temporarily hold back tics through intense concentration but later need to release them, and that this is an exhausting process. Understanding the neuroscience behind tic suppression and people's experiences with it can help those without the disorder better recognize — and have compassion for — the dynamic and sometimes demanding symptoms of Tourette syndrome. in 2019 that she lives with Tourette syndrome, internet commentators responded in two ways: Some Skeptics pointed to interviews or performances where she appeared to have no visible tics. Many concluded that she must be exaggerating or even faking her condition. But in a May 2026 interview on "Good Hang With Amy Poehler," Eilish shared how requires constantly using "everything in (her) power" to do so. Many people with Tourette syndrome often deal with , among other challenges, that have a far greater impact on with friendships and school performance. A child may be teased because of involuntary blinking or shoulder movements, but what ultimately limits that child's success may be untreated anxiety, overwhelming obsessive thoughts or difficulty sustaining attention in the classroom. What causes Tourette's is still unknown, though researchers believe , although estimates vary across studies and populations. While the disorder occurs around the globe, no two people experience Tourette syndrome in the same way. Some people have simple motor tics, such as blinking, shoulder shrugging or facial movements. Others involving multiple muscle groups or elaborate sequences of actions. Vocal tics may range from throat clearing and sniffing to repeating words or sounds. Some people develop rituals or repetitive behaviors that overlap with obsessive-compulsive symptoms, making it difficult to distinguish where a tic ends and an obsessive-compulsive behavior begins. . Each person's combination of symptoms is unique. People's tics are also dynamic. They wax and wane and are influenced by . Many people experience fewer visible tics while they are intensely focused on an activity, such as performing music or playing sports. Others say they have a dramatic increase in tics after returning home from school or work, where they can finally defining characteristics of Tourette syndrome and can lead outside observers to wonder whether a person's diagnosis is real. . People can suppress their tics for hours in situations where they fear embarrassment or judgment. Teachers or employers may conclude that the student or employee is fine. articles.title: Evidence of active volcanoes on Mars may boost chances of finding life
articles.desc: Recent fractures on the surface of Mars and gases detected by an orbiter probe provide some of the strongest evidence yet that the planet is volcanically active
articles.content: Evidence of active volcanoes on Mars may boost chances of finding life | New Scientist Mars may be volcanically active, say scientists who have linked evidence of gases often produced by magma with photographs of fresh fissures found on the surface of the Red Planet. The findings could be interpreted as good news in the hunt for life, as a continuous heat source would be needed to keep microorganisms safe from frigid temperatures on the surface. Scientists have seen evidence of volcanoes on Mars in the past few million years and seismic activity has hinted that some may still be active, but no evidence of lava flows or current eruptions had previously been found. Why we must investigate Phobos, the solar system’s strangest object In 2019, the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter detected evidence of hydrogen chloride (HCl) in Mars’s atmosphere. That gas is commonly associated with magmatic vents on Earth, and researchers wondered if the same was true on Mars. at the Polish Academy of Sciences and his colleagues looked at the little data available – just 15 recorded instances of the gas – alongside newly taken photographs of the surface. They were able to link recent, narrow fissures in the Alba Mons region of Mars to the HCl emissions, providing strong evidence of underground lava flow. To assess whether the HCl could have come from the fissures, the team modelled the wind direction at the time the measurements were taken. “We have 2 kilometres of wind between them, and in this season there are a lot of dust devils. So, the atmosphere is turbulent. It’s an enormous mess,” says Mège. at the University of Bern, Switzerland, another team member, stresses that until the area is investigated up-close, there will always be doubt about the source of the gas. But, he argues, this finding makes the case for further surface exploration of Mars. “Suspicion is one thing, proof is better, right?” says Thomas. “I’m a terrible sceptic. Until you put something down there and you actually sniff the stuff coming out of the ground, you haven’t got unambiguous proof.” Thomas thinks the finding makes the prospects for life on Mars more likely. “We know that Mars, even at the equator, can be −70°C, −80°C at night. It’s a very harsh environment,” he says. “If this thermal source were constant and continuous, then you have to admit it’s improving the situation [in terms of the hunt for life].” “This is definitely a highly interesting finding,” says at the Free University of Berlin. “Many scientists working on Mars will not be too surprised, as the picture of a ‘dead’ Mars was inconsistent with many recent research findings.” Explore the latest news, articles and features Earth extremophile can grow in near-Mars-like conditions Possible signs of ancient life on Mars are rich in complex carbon Why the lack of water on Mars is so mysterious British Iron Age ‘king’ who prompted Roman invasion was probably a woman Vibrating mattress helps clear Alzheimer’s protein from the brain Toothbrush that emits electricity may more effectively prevent gum disease We are finally pinning down what makes dyslexic brains different Humans evolved to be surprisingly fat – no wonder we struggle with dieting We’re solving the fundamental mystery of how reality is glued together Physicists get first glimpse of the zeptoverse from LHC experiment Nap schedules at childcare may not fit children’s sleep needs Inca children were drugged before being sacrificed Does Sabrina Pasterski’s holographic theory make her the next Einstein?
